title: Why Data Travels in Packets
about: Why your data is cut into small pieces before it travels.

cards.prompt:
A film streams on your Wi-Fi while you play an online game.

If the film came as **one giant piece**, what would happen to your game?

options.text: It would freeze until the whole film had arrived
Nothing: the Wi-Fi carries both side by side
options.nudge: One giant piece fills the whole connection until it's done: could anything squeeze past it?

options.text: It would run faster, as the film clears out sooner
options.nudge: The film isn't out of the way while it's still arriving: what about your game's data meanwhile?

options.text: The TV would cut the film up, so you'd never notice
options.nudge: Here the film is sent as one piece and the TV only receives it: what happens to everything else?

cards.explanation: One giant piece would hog the connection, so your game would **wait** for the whole film. That's why the internet chops data into small pieces that take turns, so both keep going.
cards.hint: Picture one enormous lorry on a single-lane road: what happens to the cars behind it?

cards.title: Numbered postcards
cards.body: So the internet chops data into **packets** that **take turns**. Each is like a numbered postcard: data (the **payload**) plus a label with the **source** address (from), the **destination** (to) and, usually, a **sequence number**. With **TCP** rules, a lost packet is resent alone.

cards.prompt: Here's one [[packet]] of a selfie you're sending. Match each part to what it's for.

pairs.right: Where the reply goes back to
Where it fits when the selfie is rebuilt

pairs.left: A strip of the selfie's pixels

cards.explanation: **From** is the source, so replies go there, and **To** is where it's heading. **#3** puts the selfie back in order, and the pixels are the **payload**, the actual data.
cards.hint: Think of the postcard: who it's from, who it's to, its number and its bit of the story.
cards.nudge: A reply goes back to whoever sent the packet; the number only puts pieces back in order.

cards.prompt: A **6,000-[[byte]]** message goes in [[packets|packet]] carrying **1,500 bytes** of data each. How many packets?
cards.explanation: 6,000 ÷ 1,500 = **4** packets. In real [[networks|network]] the label uses a little of each packet's space, so it would need one more.
cards.hint: How many 1,500-byte loads fit in 6,000 bytes?
cards.nudge: Each packet carries 1,500 bytes of the message: divide, don't multiply.

cards.prompt: Put a message's journey in order.

items.label: The message is split into small pieces
Each piece gets addresses and a number
The packets travel across the network
Receiver puts it back together by number

cards.explanation: The data is **split** first, then each piece gets its addresses and sequence number. Only after the packets arrive can the receiver rebuild the message in order.
cards.hint: A thing must exist before it's labelled, and pieces must arrive before they're rebuilt.
cards.nudge: Labels go on pieces, so the pieces must exist first; rebuilding comes at the very end.

cards.prompt: Why does the internet split data into [[packets|packet]] instead of one long stream?

options.text: Connections are shared, and TCP resends just a lost piece
Pieces make the files smaller, so they travel faster
options.nudge: Splitting doesn't shrink a file: each piece even gets a label added.

options.text: Nobody can read one small piece, so data stays secret
options.nudge: Anyone who collects all the packets can rebuild them, so nothing is hidden.

options.text: Cables carry one letter at a time, so files must split
options.nudge: Cables aren't limited to one letter: think of the film and the game sharing the Wi-Fi.

cards.explanation: Packets let many conversations **take turns** on the same connections, and with TCP only a lost piece is resent. Splitting adds labels rather than shrinking data, and hides nothing: keeping secrets is **encryption**'s job.
cards.hint: Think of the film and the game, and what happens when one piece goes missing.

cards.prompt: A file comes in 10 packets using [[TCP]] rules, and **packet 7** gets lost. What happens?

options.text: The receiver spots the gap, and only 7 is resent
The whole file is sent again from the start
options.nudge: The other nine arrived safely: only the missing piece needs sending again.

options.text: The file arrives with a hole, and nobody notices
options.nudge: The numbers jump from 6 to 8, so the receiver can tell one is missing.

options.text: The download stops, and you must restart it
options.nudge: One lost packet isn't the end: what do the numbers let the receiver ask for?

cards.explanation: The sequence numbers show a gap between 6 and 8, so under TCP the receiver tells the sender and **packet 7** is resent. The others arrived safely, so there's no need to start over.
cards.hint: Each packet carries a [[sequence number]]: what could the receiver notice when 7 never turns up?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Data travels in small pieces called **packets**.
- Each carries data plus addresses and a **sequence number**.
- Packets take turns; with **TCP**, a lost one is resent alone.
